Vancouver, BC: UBCWPL. That moon has risen: The semantics of nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives* Reed Steiner and Lisa Matthewson University of British Columbia Abstract: This paper examines the semantics of nominal demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín (Salish). We investigate the definiteness properties of the demonstratives and propose that they convey uniqueness but not familiarity. This finding adds to our cross-linguistic understanding of demonstratives, as nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives differ from demonstratives in languages like English. nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives are felicitous when their referent uniquely satisfies its nominal description, without giving rise to the ‘anti-uniqueness’ effects found in English. We further show that anti-uniqueness effects do arise in nɬeʔkepmxcín, but only when the demonstrative combines with a DP introduced by the oblique marker t. We therefore argue that this anti-uniqueness derives from semantic partitivity, and is crucially not part of the semantics or pragmatics of the demonstrative itself.
Keywords: nɬeʔkepmxcín, Salish, demonstratives, definiteness, uniqueness, partitivity

form: This paper presents a study of the semantics of nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives.1 We focus on the question of whether nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives have any definiteness properties. form: This question is of empirical interest because these semantic properties have not so far been investigated for nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives – or, to our knowledge, for demonstratives in any Salish language, except in a talk on St’át’imcets (Northern Interior Salish) by Matthewson (2022). Marianne Huijsmans (p.c.) has also begun investigating this issue in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Central Salish). Our research question is also of theoretical interest, since Salish languages, including nɬeʔkepmxcín, lack definite determiners (Matthewson 1998, 1999; Koch & Zimmermann 2010; Gillon 2014), and it has even been argued that St’át’imcets lacks any familiarity presuppositions altogether (Matthewson 2006). Yet, many analyses of demonstratives maintain that they are enriched definite descriptions (e.g., Roberts 2002; Wolter 2006; Elbourne 2008, 2013; Ahn 2019). We argue based on fieldwork with two nɬeʔkepmxcín speakers and speech data from a third speaker that nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives are weak definites in the sense of Schwarz (2009): that is, they convey uniqueness within a discourse situation, but do not convey familiarity/anaphoricity. We further show that nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives may combine either with ordinary determiner phrases (DPs) or with DPs introduced by the oblique marker t, and that this has a semantic impact. Specifically, demonstratives associated with obliques are interpreted partitively, displaying anti- uniqueness effects. We argue that the anti-uniqueness effects are not contributed by the demonstrative itself (as is often argued for English), but by the partitive oblique that follows the demonstrative.

The rest of the introductory section provides background on the language and the speakers we work with, our methodology, and the semantics of definite descriptions and demonstratives. In section 2 we introduce nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives. Section 3 presents new data on the definiteness properties of nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives and on the partitivity effect contributed by the oblique marker. Section 4 presents our informal analysis of the data, and section 5 concludes.

form: There is no single standard orthography for nɬeʔkepmxcín. Examples in this paper are presented in a variant of the North American Phonetic Alphabet as used by Thompson & Thompson (1992, 1996) and Jimmie (1994). This orthography is used by many speakers of the language, but other orthographies exist. The writing system we use does not have capital letters or punctuation marks. We elicited data from two nɬeʔkepmxcín speakers for this research: Bev Phillips (BP) and kʷaɬtèzetkʷ / Bernice Garcia (KBG). Bev Phillips was our primary consultant on this project; she is from Lytton and identifies with the ƛ̓q̓mcín (Lytton) dialect. kʷaɬtèzetkʷ is from Coldwater and identifies with the nc̕eɬétkʷu (Coldwater) dialect.2 We also draw data from some recordings of natural conversation between kʷaɬtèzetkʷ and a third speaker, c̓úʔsinek / Marty Aspinall (CMA). c̓úʔsinek is from Coldwater and identifies with the scw̓exmxcín (Nicola Valley) dialect. c̕úʔsinek was not consulted directly for logistical reasons, but her conversations were instrumental for hypothesis formation. form: Our examples were collected mostly over Zoom, but sometimes in person. We used standard semantic fieldwork methods as outlined for example in Matthewson (2004), Bohnemeyer (2015), Bochnak & Matthewson (2020) and references therein. Elicitation tasks consisted primarily of translation tasks (usually from English to nɬeʔkepmxcín) and elicited production tasks, in which the consultant was asked to produce a nɬeʔkepmxcín utterance. Both types of task always relied on prior discourse contexts: that is, the consultants were provided with a context (either verbally or in the form of pictures) and then asked to produce a nɬeʔkepmxcín utterance or translate an English utterance in that discourse context.

Examples are presented in a four-line format. The first and second lines are written in a version of the North American Phonetic Alphabet as discussed above. The first line represents the surface pronunciation and corresponds to how many community members write the language. The second line presents the underlying forms, including indicating material that is deleted either through regular morpho-phonological processes or because of fast speech. The third line is the morpheme gloss line, and the fourth is a translation into English.
1.4 Background on definiteness and demonstrative semantics

For many decades, formal semantic analyses of definite determiners proposed that they impose either uniqueness (Russell 1905; Kadmon 1990; Abbott 1999, among others) or familiarity (Christopherson 1939; Prince 1981; Heim 1982, among others). The two approaches – very roughly and informally speaking – mean that the definite determiner in (1) either requires that there be one unique dog in the discourse context, or that there be a familiar dog in the discourse context.3 (1) The dog is hungry.

As pointed out by Heim (1982) among others, familiarity in a sense relies on uniqueness. What is required in (1) is not just that there be any number of familiar dogs in the discourse context, but that there be one familiar dog that is identifiable to the addressee.

A new line of research emerged with work by Schwarz (2009) (and earlier work by Ebert 1971 on Fering). Schwarz argues, primarily based on German, that languages can lexically distinguish unique from familiar definite determiners. Schwarz calls unique definites ‘weak’ and familiar definites ‘strong’. In line with the fact that familiarity entails uniqueness, in Schwarz’s analysis ‘[t]he strong article is made up of the meaning of the weak article plus an anaphoric index argument’ (Schwarz 2009:137). Since then, a productive line of research has begun investigating how weak vs. strong definite determiners are manifested in various languages; see for example Arkoh and Matthewson (2013), Jenks (2018), and Royer (2022).
3 Uncited English examples in this paper were generated by the authors.

Schwarz proposes several diagnostics to distinguish between weak and strong definites, in addition to the core properties of whether they require only uniqueness, or also familiarity. Among these is a distinction in which types of bridging the two types of definites allow. Bridging is a phenomenon whereby definites are licensed through inferences derived from previous material. The two types of bridging (part-whole and relational anaphora) are illustrated for English in (2)- (3). In the part-whole bridging in (2), the steering wheel is rendered unique in the context by the previous mention of a car, since cars each have exactly one steering wheel. In the relational anaphora bridging case in (3), the author is licensed because the previous mention of a book entails the existence of that book’s author.

form: (2) I bought a new car. The steering wheel is purple. PART-WHOLE BRIDGING (3) I read a good book. I wrote to the author. RELATIONAL ANAPHORA BRIDGING Schwarz shows that in German, part-whole bridging uses a weak definite determiner, while relational anaphora bridging uses a strong determiner. We will use these bridging diagnostics, among other diagnostics, in section 3 when probing the semantics of nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives. When it comes to the semantics of demonstratives, Royer (2022:190) points out that the literature has ‘widely assumed that [they] are a sub-type of definite article’ – and often, specifically a strong definite article. See Wolter (2006), Schwarz (2013), Simonenko (2014), Jenks (2015), Šimík (2016), Bombi (2018), Ahn (2019), Hanink (2021), Patel-Grosz & Grosz (2017) and Kim (2024), among others, for discussion.

Interestingly, although many authors view demonstratives as imposing strong definiteness, and although strong definiteness (familiarity) is usually taken to also entail uniqueness, English demonstratives actually display anti-uniqueness effects, as illustrated in (4).
(4) a. The/ #That sun is made of hydrogen and helium.
(Robinson 2005:51, cited in Saha 2025:1384) b. The/ #That author of Waverley also wrote Ivanhoe.

(Nowak 2019:2867, cited in Saha 2025:1384) c. The/ #That current president of India is Droupadi Murmu. (Saha 2025:1384) The status of the anti-uniqueness effects is a matter of debate, with some authors proposing that it is a presupposition (e.g., Nowak 2019, Dayal & Jiang 2022, Owusu 2022, Saha 2025), and others proposing that it is only an implicature or arises through competition with the definite article (e.g. Blumberg 2020; Ahn 2019, 2023). One recurring idea that helps explain the conflict between the uniqueness required by definites and the anti-uniqueness of demonstratives is that demonstratives require uniqueness within a smaller situation and anti-uniqueness within a larger situation (or in a different possible world); see for example Wolter (2006), Dayal & Jiang (2022), Saha (2025).

form: We assume that demonstratives never replace determiners in nɬeʔkepmxcín, but always co- occur with determiners when appearing with a nominal restriction. This differs from some Central Salish languages, e.g. ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Reisinger & Huijsmans 2021). Cases seen below where there is no audible determiner are analyzed as underlyingly containing the determiner (h)e=, which is often reduced or dropped (Koch 2004:270), especially after a word ending in a vowel (Kroeber 1997:379; see also Thompson & Thompson 1992:146).5 Nominal demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín form a syntactic constituent with their DP or oblique phrase. There are two main pieces of evidence for this. First, the entire phrase can be left-dislocated as a single unit, as shown in (6). Assuming this left-peripheral internal topic position can only be occupied by one phrase at a time (Koch 2006), this is evidence of constituency.
Context: Your friend’s bag catches on a nail and starts to tear.
'This bag will rip if I fill it up.'

(more literally: This bag, it will rip if I fill it up.) (VF | KBG 23 April 2025) The second piece of evidence supporting constituency is that demonstratives always follow quantifiers; they cannot precede them.6 This rigid ordering would be difficult to explain if the quantifier formed a constituent with the DP, but the demonstrative did not.
Context: There are several broken baskets. You’re asked if you’re gonna fix them today.
‘I’m gonna fix all of these baskets.’

form: In this section we apply a range of definiteness diagnostics to the nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives. In section 3.2, we investigate whether demonstratives are acceptable in non-unique contexts. In section 3.3, we explore whether the demonstratives are compatible with immediate situation uniqueness. Section 3.4 looks at larger situation uniqueness, and 3.5 examines global uniqueness. In Section 3.6 we look at part-whole bridging, and in Section 3.7 at relational anaphora bridging. Section 3.8 discusses some variable cases and exceptions. In Section 3.9 we summarize the generalizations.

Based on textual data alone, it is unclear whether these are nominal or adverbial demonstratives. We hypothesize that ɬʔé is proximal and ɬéʔe is distal, in line with the evidence-neutral demonstratives (proximal xʔé and distal xéʔe) and with demonstrative adverbs (e.g. proximal nʔé and distal néʔe), but the precise semantics of these demonstratives is currently unknown to linguistics.

In brief, the data will show that nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives do not enforce familiarity and they do not in themselves have anti-uniqueness effects, similar to St'át'imcets (Matthewson 2022). They are compatible with an analysis according to which they convey weak definiteness (uniqueness). The data further reveal the novel finding that demonstratives with non-oblique DPs are semantically different from demonstratives with oblique DPs, with only the latter requiring anti- uniqueness.

The first diagnostic we examine involves contexts where the referent is not unique in the immediate speech situation. We test this in (8), where two identical cups are presented to the consultant at an equal distance from the researcher, and the researcher asks the consultant to take a cup without gesturing or differentiating either cup from the other. In this context, only a plain DP is acceptable, marked with an oblique in (8a) as expected of the patient of an unergative predicate. It is not acceptable to use a demonstrative with a plain DP (8b) or a demonstrative with an oblique (8c).
Context: Researcher holds two identical cups at an equal distance and asks for the consultant to take one without gesturing.

This is evidence that demonstratives identify a unique referent. If a referent is not unique, and no gesture is used to pick out a unique referent, then the demonstrative is not acceptable. But if a gesture is used to create uniqueness, the demonstrative becomes acceptable. See section 4.2.2 for further discussion.

The second definiteness diagnostic we look at is whether the relevant phrase is felicitous in immediate situation unique contexts.8 These are contexts in which the discourse participants know that there is exactly one individual of the relevant type in the immediate situation of their conversation (cf. Schwarz 2009:21). In languages that distinguish definites from indefinites, definites will be not only felicitous, but required, in such contexts. This can be seen for English in (10). In a language that distinguishes weak from strong definites, the prediction is that the weak definite would be used in these contexts, since uniqueness is satisfied but familiarity is not: the bed has not previously been mentioned.

Context: You have exactly one bed in your bedroom. You walk into your bedroom and notice something unusual. You say: The/#a bed is broken! In languages with no definite/indefinite distinction, such as St’át’imcets, an indefinite determiner is licensed in immediate situation unique contexts. This is shown in (11). The lake has not previously been mentioned in the story, and is therefore not familiar in the discourse, but it is uniquely identifiable. 8 The term goes back to Hawkins (1978), as does the term ‘larger situation’ uniqueness, discussed in the next sub-section.
Context: He got to the top of Mission Mountain.

The clear trend is towards the generalization that xéʔe with a plain DP is compatible with immediate situation uniqueness and xéʔe with an oblique is not. The variation that exists could reflect a dialect difference or a change in progress, but it is also likely to at least partly be due to the extreme context-sensitivity of the effects. All it takes to alleviate anti-uniqueness is for a speaker to enrich the context slightly in their minds, and this may tend to happen more for some consultants than for others.

The felicity of demonstratives with plain DPs in contexts involving immediate situation uniqueness supports our proposal that they are weak definites: in these contexts, uniqueness is satisfied, but not familiarity. The infelicity of (or dispreference for) demonstratives with obliques in these contexts suggests that the oblique adds an anti-uniqueness requirement.

The fourth definiteness diagnostic we look at is whether the relevant phrase is felicitous in larger situation unique contexts. These are contexts in which the discourse participants know there is exactly one individual of the relevant type in a larger situation, outside of the immediate situation of their conversation (see for example Schwarz 2009:21). For languages that distinguish definites from indefinites, the definite determiner is predicted to be obligatory in large situation uniqueness contexts, and the indefinite determiner is predicted to be infelicitous. And demonstratives that require anti-uniqueness are predicted to be infelicitous here. This can be seen for English in (18). (18) The/#a/#that prime minister is in Vancouver today.

form: In this section we investigate whether demonstratives can refer to individuals that are unique in the global situation, e.g. astronomical bodies like the moon and sun. Cross-linguistically, definites that relate to globally unique individuals do not necessarily pattern in the same way as other larger- situation unique definites (see e.g. Simpson and Biswas 2016 on Bangla; Gao 2025 on Wu).12 In nɬeʔkepmxcín, judgements vary when the referent is globally unique. For BP, globally unique entities pattern the same way as other unique entities: demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, and demonstratives with obliques are not. For kʷałtèzetkʷ, judgements vary between sessions. In some sessions, she patterns like BP: demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, and demonstratives with obliques are not. In other sessions, all demonstratives are unacceptable in globally unique contexts.

form: kʷałtèzetkʷ's variation can be explained pragmatically. If demonstratives signify uniqueness, and astronomical bodies are globally unique, then demonstratives are redundant and uncommunicative in most contexts. This explains why demonstratives are rejected in (26b) and (27b). However, because this is a pragmatic effect, demonstratives do not contradict the description given by the DP, which explains why she sometimes accepts them in (25b), and why she acknowledges her own variation in comments on (27c).

In part-whole bridging contexts, a definite description is used for some unique sub-part (the ‘part’) of a unique individual that was already introduced in the context (the ‘whole’). Even if the part has not yet been mentioned, it can still be uniquely identified through its relationship to the whole. The part does not have to be familiar, but it does have to be unique.

In languages with a definiteness contrast, definites are required for part-whole bridging, and indefinites are infelicitous. Morphemes that induce anti-uniqueness are also infelicitous. This is shown for English in (28).

form: Schwarz (2009) predicts that weak/uniqueness definites are licensed by part-whole bridging, while strong/familiarity definites are not. According to Ahn & Zhu (2025:435), demonstratives are generally assumed to be incompatible with bridging; however, they show that Mandarin demonstratives are compatible with part-whole bridging.16 If the nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives are uniqueness definites as in our proposal, we predict that they will be compatible with part-whole bridging.

Our investigation reveals that nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives are possible with part-whole bridging, as predicted. Data are provided in (29)-(31). As with previous data, demonstratives with obliques are rejected with unique referents.17

16 Wolter (2006:76) observes that in English, demonstratives are only licensed in bridging contexts when they are contrastively focused. In bridging contexts, a definite determiner is licensed and when all else is equal, the definite is preferred. In contrastive contexts, demonstratives are licit as there is uniqueness within a smaller situation. See related discussion in section 4.

17 Readers may notice that in (29), the roof-phrase has possessive marking, and in subsequent testing with the same consultant it was revealed that the possessive cannot felicitously be removed. form: The final definiteness diagnostic we tested involves relational anaphora bridging. Typically, relational anaphora bridging requires a relational noun (such as author); see Schwarz (2009:129- 131). nɬeʔkepmxcín doesn’t have many relational nouns, so this type of bridging is a little challenging to test, but we have included some borrowings from English, as well as headless relative clauses, which are how English relational nouns are often paraphrased.

Despite this variation, relational anaphora contexts provide good evidence that demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín are agnostic to familiarity. If demonstratives with plain DPs can be used for part- whole bridging (§3.6) and relational anaphora bridging (§3.7), then familiarity does not impact their acceptability.

For BP, relational anaphora contexts also provide good evidence that demonstratives with obliques require anti-uniqueness to be felicitous. They can be used neither for part-whole bridging (§3.6) nor for relational anaphora bridging (§3.7). What both kinds of bridging have in common is that the definite description must be unique. If demonstratives with obliques are acceptable in neither context, then it must be the uniqueness of the referent that causes infelicity.

We have seen so far that demonstratives with obliques are generally unacceptable when the referent is unique, but there are a number of exceptional cases. The first consistent exception involves gradable adjective predicates (§3.8.1). The second consistent exception involves sub-part readings (§3.8.2). There are also exceptional cases we have yet to fully explain, which may involve gesture, joint attention, and spatially disjoined situations (§3.8.3). Exceptions are unsurprising, since demonstratives are highly discourse and context sensitive, but more research is needed to explain these precise sensitivities.

form: Gradable adjectives (e.g. tall, short, long, pretty) imply comparison. For instance, the English adjective tall is true of someone who is six feet tall in the context of a social gathering, but false of that same person in the context of a professional basketball team. Evaluating whether a gradable adjective is true requires comparison against some standard, which depends on the context. form: On the surface, these cases seem to violate anti-uniqueness, since there is no other individual in the immediate context of the utterance that matches the description. However, this anti- uniqueness violation is only surface-level. By comparing the individual against some standard degree of comparison, the gradable adjective implies some baseline individual which meets that standard. How to best formalize this effect remains to be worked out, but the empirical generalization remains that comparison implies non-uniqueness.

form: To summarize, nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives signify uniqueness, and demonstratives with obliques require anti-uniqueness. Demonstratives are always illicit when there is no uniquely identifiable referent, and they are always acceptable when a gesture is used to identify a unique referent from a larger set (section 3.2). Where demonstratives with plain DPs and demonstratives with obliques differ is in unique contexts, where the referent is already unique and does not need to be isolated from a larger set. In general, plain DPs without a demonstrative are preferred unless the demonstrative adds some new information. But whereas a demonstrative with a plain DP is redundant in these contexts, a demonstrative with an oblique is entirely illicit. In immediate situation unique contexts, where the referent is already unique in the immediate speech situation, demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, but demonstratives with obliques are categorically rejected (section 3.3). In larger situation unique contexts, where the referent is not necessarily present in the immediate situation, but is known to be unique in the larger situation, demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, but demonstratives with obliques are rejected (section 3.4). In contexts where the referent is known to be globally unique, demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, but demonstratives with obliques are rejected, except for some speakers who reject all demonstratives outright on some occasions (section 3.5). In bridging contexts, where the referent is uniquely identifiable through some other DP introduced earlier in the discourse, demonstratives with plain DPs are acceptable, and demonstratives with obliques are unacceptable (sections 3.6-3.7). All these data points support the generalization that demonstratives with plain DPs signify uniqueness, and demonstratives with obliques require anti-uniqueness. The systematic exceptions support this conclusion. Demonstratives with obliques are exceptionally permitted with gradable adjective predicates because the standard of comparison implies another individual and satisfies the anti-uniqueness requirement (§3.8.1). Demonstratives with obliques are also exceptionally permitted with a sub-part reading, where they refer to only one subpart of a larger whole (§3.8.2). This supports the hypothesis that demonstratives with obliques strictly identify some unique individual or part from a larger set or larger individual within which they are non-unique: if the individual is also unique in that larger set, the demonstrative with an oblique is ill-formed.

form: Broadly speaking, when talking about a specific individual, a nɬeʔkepmxcín speaker has at least three options: a plain DP, a demonstrative with a plain DP, or a demonstrative with an oblique. Plain DPs we argue signify neither uniqueness nor familiarity: following Matthewson (2022) on St’át’imcets, we tentatively assume they are of type <e,t> and combine with a phonologically null choice function that returns a specific individual (section 4.1). When demonstratives combine with a plain DP, they replace the choice function, and return a unique individual which is not necessarily familiar (section 4.2). Obliques modifying demonstratives function as partitives: they introduce a proper superset of individuals containing the referent of the demonstrative (section 4.3). The three options available to a speaker interact with one another, which introduces competition effects.

form: We have not undertaken targeted investigation of plain DPs – in other words, of the semantics of determiners – in nɬeʔkepmxcín. However, we assume following Koch & Zimmermann (2010:239) that nɬeʔkepmxcín “[d]eterminers do not encode a definite/indefinite-distinction, nor a uniqueness presupposition”. This means that all plain DPs are indefinites. Due to the absence of any contrasting definite plain DPs, these indefinite plain DPs can be used in contexts that satisfy uniqueness and/or familiarity. They do not, however, require either uniqueness or familiarity.

form: An interesting question for future research is why plain DPs are good in bridging contexts (see sections 3.6 and 3.7). If demonstratives plus plain DPs encode uniqueness, and plain DPs alone do not, we might expect demonstratives to be preferred in bridging contexts, which crucially rely on uniqueness (and which do not allow indefinites in English, for example). Potential avenues to explore in explaining this behavior could involve the specificity of plain DPs (if indeed, they are specific, as they are in St’át’imcets), or perhaps plain determiners do not pragmatically compete with demonstratives when it comes to uniqueness, since they have different deictic properties.

Because demonstratives can undergo syntactic movement to second position, they are likely generated as adjuncts or specifiers to the DP. Matthewson & Davis (1995) argue against the adjunction analysis for St’át’imcets: if demonstratives were adjoined to DPs, then there would be nothing to prevent the inner DP from containing a quantifier, which incorrectly predicts that demonstratives should be acceptable before quantifiers. This works for St’át’imcets, but there are two reasons to prefer the adjunction analysis for nɬeʔkepmxcín.

It is unclear how robust these judgements are, and BP does reject this word order (see 7b. above). form: We propose that nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives have the semantics of weak definites, in the sense of Schwarz (2009): they enforce uniqueness within a situation, but do not impose a familiarity requirement. Thus, a demonstrative + plain DP phrase like xéʔe e sqáqx̣aʔ ‘that dog’ picks out the unique dog within a relevant discourse situation. Importantly, as argued by Wolter (2006) among many others, the uniqueness imposed by demonstratives is not required to hold within the entire discourse situation within which definite articles are evaluated. Deictic gestures such as pointing are able to narrow down the domain, picking out a smaller situation within which the uniqueness is verified. In Wolter’s terminology, demonstratives enforce uniqueness within a ‘non-default’ situation.

The relevance of deictic gestures in narrowing the situation within which the referent is unique is illustrated in (51). In (51a), there are two cats in the speech situation, and the consultant indicates that pointing is necessary to license the demonstrative. In (51b), the consultant volunteers a demonstrative (with an oblique) in a situation where each child is being pointed at.

form: In English, such narrowing to a non-default situation is normally infelicitous for globally unique entities such as the moon. For ordinary reference to a unique entity of this sort, the definite article is a better choice and therefore must be chosen. If one does use a demonstrative when talking about the moon, a pragmatically non-default inference arises, such as an emotive/affective effect. This competition between demonstratives and definites can also explain the anti-uniqueness effect of English demonstratives: reference is to an entity which is unique within the smaller, non-default situation, but because the definite article was not chosen, there is non-uniqueness in the larger, default situation.

Now, it might seem that we cannot directly use an analysis along these lines for nɬeʔkepmxcín. The two languages differ: as we have shown, in nɬeʔkepmxcín, unlike in English, demonstratives are felicitous in contexts of larger situation uniqueness and even of global uniqueness, such as when referring to the moon.

However, an independent difference between the languages provides the clue to the cross- linguistic variation. Unlike English, nɬeʔkepmxcín lacks any definite determiner like the. Thus, according to our proposal, demonstratives are the only elements in nɬeʔkepmxcín which enforce uniqueness, and there is no competition with any other uniqueness-imposing element as there is in English. Notice further that even though nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives allow narrowing of the situation in which the uniqueness is evaluated, this narrowing is semantically vacuous in larger- situation uniqueness contexts. Given that the moon is globally unique, for example, it makes no difference if we also claim that it is unique within a smaller situation – perhaps one narrowed down by a deictic gesture. The redundancy brought in by adding a demonstrative to an already-unique referent can also explain the fact, illustrated many times above, that speakers prefer to use plain DPs rather than DPs with demonstratives unless there is a particular reason to focus attention on a specific referent.

Turning briefly to familiarity, our proposal predicts that nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives are agnostic with respect this concept. Since the demonstratives do not impose familiarity, they should be fine when referring to novel individuals. And since there is no competing familiarity-requiring element in the language, demonstratives with plain DPs should also be fine when referring to familiar individuals. This is the case, as seen in the examples above – which mostly involve novel referents – and in the familiar referent example in (52):

form: We very briefly sketch an idea about how this proposal might work compositionally. The demonstrative is of type <<e,t>,e>, like a choice function. It applies to a set-denoting plain DP and picks out the unique referent that satisfies the plain DP predicate within a non-default situation. It also adds deictic or evidential information.

We analyze demonstrative with obliques as partitives, and provide an incomplete sketch of an analysis here. Assuming the oblique marker is a preposition, we tentatively propose the structure in (53).23 This analysis is a work in progress.
23 Henry Davis observes (p.c.) that this idea makes predictions about Condition C effects, which we have not had time to test yet.

The oblique PP is a function of type <e,t>, which holds of any individual that satisfies the DP predicate it contains (i.e. in this case, individuals who are women), and which moreover is a proper subpart of the set of salient such individuals in the discourse situation. In this example, the oblique PP picks out the set of individuals who are women and who are a proper subpart of the set of salient women. This proper subpart relation will derive the anti-uniqueness effects (cf. Barker 1998:679: “partitivity is always proper partitivity”.) We further suggest that the oblique PP adjoins to a silent pronoun, and the demonstrative adjoins to the [pro + oblique] constituent. The pronoun identifies the set of salient individuals in a situation s. The pro-DP and the oblique PP combine by Predicate Modification (Heim & Kratzer 1998), giving an intersective meaning. The [pro + oblique] constituent denotes the set of individuals who are salient in the discourse situation, are women, and are a proper subpart of the salient women. The demonstrative then chooses a particular individual from this set.

Crucially, pro and the complement of the oblique preposition are evaluated relative to two separate situations. pro is evaluated relative to a non-default, narrowed situation. The complement of the oblique preposition is evaluated relative to a more general situation. This allows the referent of the entire phrase to be unique in a gesture situation, but non-unique in the broader context. Note that the fact that the two situations are distinct is enforced not by the demonstrative itself, but by the partitive relation brought in by the oblique. The non-default pro-situation must be smaller than the situation of the complement of the oblique; otherwise, the set of salient individuals denoted by pro could not be a proper subpart of the set of salient women denoted by the PP. One analytically unfavourable side-effect of this analysis is that pro must be of type <e,t> to compose with the demonstrative, rather than a variable of type e. This means that pro, like other DPs, would have to compose with either a silent choice function or a demonstrative to saturate an argument position. A similar silent nominal has been proposed for partitives in European languages (Falco and Zamparelli 2019, Jackendoff 1977).
This analysis is tentative and not worked out in detail yet. There are various other options for the syntactic structure and the semantics; further research is required.

form: In this paper we have argued that nɬeʔkepmxcín nominal demonstratives are weak definites in the sense of Schwarz (2009): they convey uniqueness. This uniqueness is required to hold within a non-default situation, often a situation smaller than the entire speech situation and indicated by a deictic gesture. However, this narrowing of the situation can – unlike in languages like English – be semantically vacuous, thus allowing nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives to be used, at least for some speakers, even when referring to globally unique entities such as the moon.

We also uncovered anti-uniqueness effects with nɬeʔkepmxcín demonstratives, but these are systematically present when, and only when, the demonstrative combines with an oblique phrase rather than a plain DP. We proposed that these cases are explicit partitive constructions: the oblique marker introduces a necessarily proper superset of entities matching the description provided by the NP. Thus, we argue that there is a cross-linguistic difference between languages like English, where the demonstrative itself (and/or the demonstrative’s pragmatic competition with another form such as a definite article) contributes anti-uniqueness inferences, and languages like nɬeʔkepmxcín, where anti-uniqueness is contributed by an explicit partitive structure. Much work remains to be done. One urgent goal is to better understand the inter-speaker variation we detected. The variation is constrained and non-random: while one speaker consistently patterns in the way summarized here, the other speaker also tends in this direction, and never offers judgements going in the opposite direction. The type of judgments required in this research are extremely context-dependent, and it remains to be determined to what extent our results indicate systematic variation in the grammars of the speakers, as opposed to relative lenience and/or propensity to mentally enrich discourse contexts that are given in elicitation.
We also look forward to broader cross-Salish comparisons in future work by other researchers.
